summary: Requires, as a Best Current Practice, that DNS messages be allowed to travel over TCP on the Internet, including unencrypted TCP and TLS. This matches the implementation requirements of RFC 7766. It discusses consequences and the operational issues that arise when it is not followed. It updates RFC 1123 and RFC 1536.

eli5.summary: DNS answers can come by a fast path or a sturdy path. Networks must leave the sturdy one open too.

questions: should firewalls allow dns over tcp
should firewalls block dns over tcp
why does dns fall back to tcp
subtitle: Why blocking DNS over TCP breaks things, and why operators must allow it alongside UDP.

tldr.problem: Many operators came to believe that DNS over TCP is unneeded or unsafe and filtered it, which causes communication failures and hard-to-debug problems when answers are too large for UDP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC makes it a Best Current Practice that all DNS resolvers and servers support and service both UDP and TCP, that network operators allow both, and it gives guidance on managing TCP connections and monitoring.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 1123 and RFC 1536 and is the operational companion to the implementation requirements of RFC 7766. Filtering DNS over TCP is called harmful in the general case.

today: RFC 9210 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 235) and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 1123 and RFC 1536.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DNS messages are carried over UDP or TCP. Most transactions use UDP, and some operators have been led to believe that DNS over TCP is unwanted or unnecessary. When it is restricted, a variety of communication failures and debugging challenges often arise.

The DNS standards already require TCP support in implementations (RFC 7766). This RFC is the equivalent for the operational community: it urges system administrators, network engineers and security staff to make DNS over TCP as well supported as DNS over UDP. It updates RFC 1123 so that all resolvers and recursive servers must support both transports, and updates RFC 1536 to remove the idea that TCP is only useful for zone transfers.
sections.eli5: Some network keepers thought the sturdy truck road was never needed and closed it. This RFC says to keep both roads open.

sections.title: How UDP Came to Dominate
sections.content:
The original DNS specifications allow either transport but prefer UDP for queries because of lower overhead. RFC 1123 said resolvers MUST support UDP and SHOULD support TCP for non-zone-transfer queries, and by RFC 1536 TCP had come to be associated mainly with zone transfers. The original DNS-over-UDP maximum message size was 512 bytes.

Growing messages were expected to push traffic to TCP, through dynamic updates and DNSSEC. In practice DNS over TCP stayed little used, and EDNS(0) let senders announce a larger UDP payload size, typically within a 512- to 4096-byte range. As of 2014 DNS-over-TCP transactions were still a very small fraction of traffic at root name servers.

Large UDP messages are fragmented, and middleboxes and firewalls often block fragments. For IPv4 on a 1500-byte MTU, the largest unfragmented UDP DNS message is likely 1472 bytes. For IPv6, the RFC notes about one-third of recursive resolvers use the 1280-byte minimum MTU, and some 35% of IPv6-capable resolvers were unable to receive a fragmented packet. When data does not fit, a server sets the truncated flag and the client retries over TCP.

A belief grew that "only zone transfers use TCP" and that filtering all DNS over TCP is a best practice. Early name servers did offer little TCP connection management, but modern standards and implementations are nearing parity with what HTTP(S) servers and load balancers do. The RFC also notes that TCP can suffer head-of-line blocking from a single lost segment.
sections.eli5: Postcards were quicker, so people used them for almost everything and forgot about the truck. But when a message is too big for a postcard, or the post office throws away pieces of it, the truck is the only way.

sections.title: The DNS-over-TCP Requirement
sections.content:
The RFC rewrites two lines of RFC 1123, Section 6.1.3.2. The old text said resolvers MUST support UDP and SHOULD support TCP. The new text says all DNS resolvers and servers MUST support and service both UDP and TCP queries. Servers, including forwarders, must serve TCP so clients can reliably get large responses, and clients must support TCP so they can retry truncated UDP responses.

A server may still limit the resources it devotes to queries, but now MUST NOT refuse a query just because it would have succeeded with another transport. In RFC 1536, the statement that UDP is the chosen protocol and TCP is used for zone transfers is deleted.

The RFC concludes that filtering DNS over TCP is harmful in the general case. Resolver and server operators MUST support both transports, and network operators MUST allow both.
sections.eli5: The old rule said you could skip the truck. The new rule says every DNS helper must handle both postcards and trucks, and the road owners must let both through.

sections.title: Managing TCP Connections
sections.content:
TCP costs state, so the RFC gives operational advice. Clients MAY track and limit connection attempts to a server and use a short timeout on unestablished connections, since the operating system default is often around 60 to 120 seconds. Servers can resist SYN flooding with SYN cookies, and services not meant for the public Internet, such as most recursive servers, SHOULD be protected with access controls. Networks and applications MUST NOT refuse TCP queries that were not preceded by a UDP query.

Servers SHOULD enable TCP Fast Open, which saves one round trip, and servers behind a shared address SHOULD use the same TFO key on all instances or disable TFO on all.

Servers SHOULD actively manage connections: keep application limits lower than operating system limits, provide a configurable idle timeout, and signal timeouts with the edns-tcp-keepalive option. They MAY limit connections per source address, transactions per connection and connection duration. Clients should be ready to re-establish connections and retry. It is generally better for clients to close connections, so servers do not pile up sockets in TIME_WAIT, and changing TIME_WAIT-related settings is NOT RECOMMENDED in most cases.

DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) uses TCP port 853, and this document applies equally to it. TLS adds processing cost and, for TLS 1.3, one extra round trip on unoptimized setup.

As starting points for administrators who are unsure, the RFC says default connection limits in open-source servers range from 20 to 150, with 150 reasonable when most queries use UDP and 5000 when most use TCP or TLS. It suggests 25 connections per source address as a starting point if a limit is needed, and notes idle timeout defaults of 2 to 30 seconds, with 10 seconds reasonable.
sections.eli5: Trucks take more parking space than postcards. So a busy depot should limit how many trucks wait around and send idle ones home after a short while.

sections.title: Risks of Filtering DNS over TCP
sections.content:
A DNS answer may require TCP because of large messages, lack of EDNS(0) support, or DDoS mitigation such as Response Rate Limiting, or because of a future feature not yet foreseen. Networks that filter DNS over TCP risk losing access to significant parts of the DNS namespace, and past success with UDP cannot be guaranteed between autonomous systems.

One example is a resolver that gets a truncated reply from an authoritative server, retries over TCP, and finds TCP blocked. The pending connections consume resources until they time out, and the resolver wastes effort on queries that can never be answered.

Another is the root zone KSK rollover. During some phases, DNSKEY responses were larger than 1280 bytes, which raised concern for servers unable to receive large UDP messages or TCP. The RFC reports that during the postponed rollover there were no reported problems attributable to the 1414-octet response, nor during the period with the revoked old key and a 1425-octet response.
sections.eli5: If the truck road is blocked, a helper keeps waiting for a delivery that will never come, and some addresses cannot be reached at all.

sections.title: Logging, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Logging and monitoring tools SHOULD NOT ignore TCP. Otherwise attacks, exfiltration attempts and normal traffic may go undetected. DNS messages over TCP may arrive in many small segments, and a clever attacker may split them to hide, so packet-capture tools SHOULD reassemble the full TCP stream and limit the memory used to track connections. The RFC names dnscap and dnstap as examples.

On security, the RFC notes the irony that returning truncated UDP answers to push clients to TCP has become a common response to spoofed DNS denial-of-service attacks. UDP-based flooding is called the most common protocol attack on the DNS, though a high rate of short-lived TCP transactions may still pose challenges. It also cites research on IP fragmentation attacks when the IP Identifier is predictable. Sharing a TFO key across a server pool carries the caveat that compromising one server reveals the shared key.

On privacy, the message content is the same over either transport, but TCP details such as initial sequence numbers, window size and options might allow fingerprinting of clients. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Watchers who guard the road must check the trucks too, not just the postcards, or sneaky things can ride through unseen.
